rule: published artifacts stay byte-identical; corrections are appended

entries.source_section_or_line: N2 -- kappa-chi null on hand-built synthetic data
entries.old_statement: the kappa-chi estimator returns mean -0.093 sd 0.872, 90% interval [-1.52, +0.92], on constant-lambda data -- an interval containing every value both lanes published (ERR-HU-021)
entries.corrected_statement: That null's noise level was chosen by hand and is 27x TOO WIDE.  Rebuilt on the REAL (dV, dP) pairs with per-T residual resampling -- real tails, real per-T scatter, real counts, identical binning -- the constant-lambda null gives sd 0.029-0.032 and a 95% interval of about [-0.06, +0.06] on all three symbols.  The real values 0.2245 / 0.3786 / 0.2032 sit 7 to 13 sigma OUTSIDE it.  A recovery test on the same construction returns a known 0.25 with bias +0.003 to +0.004.  Verdict 3/3 SUPPORTED.  ERR-HU-021's reading is SUPERSEDED: the concern was legitimate to raise, the answer is that kappa-chi survives.  GENERAL LESSON, recorded because it nearly cost a correct result: AN UNCALIBRATED NULL IS AS DANGEROUS AS NO NULL -- it can kill a true finding as easily as rescue a false one.

entries.source_section_or_line: N1 -- gamma null on i.i.d. signs
entries.old_statement: gamma's null sd is 0.544, so the precision of gamma = 0.373 / 0.369 is void (ERR-HU-022)
entries.corrected_statement: The same miscalibration risk applies: that null was run where C(l) is PURE NOISE, whereas the real C(100) = 0.083 sits about 145 standard errors from zero with fit r2 0.98-0.99.  A null built where the signal is absent does not measure the estimator's precision where the signal is strong -- C-T27 has just demonstrated exactly that failure mode for kappa-chi, 27x over.  ERR-HU-022's claim that gamma's PRECISION is void is therefore SUSPENDED, not withdrawn: it stands only until gamma gets the same real-data null-plus-recovery treatment kappa-chi just received.  Its other content -- that the null is n-independent, and that the levels are not void -- is unaffected.
